source.title: Accuracy of Neural Networks for Surrogate Modelling of the Sag of Hanging Cables

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It sweeps network width and training-set size and reports test RMSE, addressing the double-descent and more-data claims on a different engineering task and with different settings from the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-RMSE results for width and sample-size sweeps. Results cited from Belkin et al. are not cataloged. The paper also reports comparisons of network depth and initialization, but those do not test the listed claim versions and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps single-hidden-layer ReLU width and training-set size on a noiseless engineering regression task and reports test RMSE. This is a new setting with its own result on model-wise double descent and the sample-size axis. It is not a reproduction of the originals' recipe, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that accuracy is non-monotonic in the number of neurons and that log-scaling was the most effective way to improve accuracy. They interpret the results as a bias domain and a variance domain, split at about 10 samples per neuron. In the variance domain, error rises to the interpolation threshold and then falls, which they explain as ensemble-like averaging in double descent. More samples reduce overfitting. Double descent is clearly described only for the log-scaled model.
record.recipe_differences: This is an engineering surrogate-model study using ReLU networks, deterministic targets, Latin-hypercube samples, and LBFGS; it does not report an explicit reproduction of the original double-descent experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The width-related pattern differs between linearly scaled and log-scaled inputs. The reported tests also vary training-set size and width; the paper describes a rough boundary of approximately 10 samples per neuron.
record.problems: The evidence is specific to one deterministic engineering problem and a particular training setup. Numerical curve values are presented in figures rather than tabulated; the text gives qualitative descriptions. Width sweeps are mainly for single-hidden-layer networks, and the results differ with input scaling.
record.rows_left_out: Section 3.1 and Figure 3 report sample-size effects for a fixed 10-neuron network, and Section 3.3/Figure 6 report the corresponding log-scaled condition: errors decrease with more samples and then plateau. These fixed-width results do not test whether more samples raise error near the interpolation threshold, so they were not extracted as claim-version rows. Figure 5 compares depth arrangements at fixed total neuron count, not a size-wise double-descent sweep.

untested.parts: Deep (multi-layer) networks. All width sweeps use a single hidden layer, and Figure 5 varies depth only at a fixed neuron count.
Model classes other than neural networks. RBF/SVM models are mentioned in the conclusion with no capacity sweep.
Noisy targets and per-sample-count curves at widths other than 10 neurons, beyond the Figure 8 heatmap.

missing.what: Sample-size sweep at fixed width: test RMSE falls monotonically (about 1/sqrt(N) up to ~1000 samples) then plateaus. There is no rise near ~100 samples, where the sample count matches the parameter count. This bears on V3 (absent), and rows_left_out wrongly says it does not cross the threshold.
missing.locator: Section 3.1, Figure 3 (linear); Section 3.3, Figure 6 (log-scaled); 1 hidden layer of 10 neurons

record.verdict_notes: The targets are noiseless, yet a peak appears (log-scaled case); the authors attribute it to variance from overfitting. This is compatible with V6's 'label noise or variance' wording, so no V6 label is given. The networks use scikit-learn 0.20.3 defaults with LBFGS. That implies an L2 penalty (alpha=1e-4) and a capped iteration count. Whether models actually interpolate is not verified, which may explain the weak or absent peaks in the linear case. All evidence is figure-only or qualitative, with distributions over 1000 initializations.

versions.untested_parts: Width sweeps are reported mainly for single-hidden-layer networks; the paper does not test the size-wise shape across deep-network architectures generally.
Training epochs or test error over training time are not swept.
The sample-size sweep does not establish that more data raises error for every setting near the interpolation threshold.
Only neural networks are studied; other model classes and the broader cross-class generalization are not tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study assumes deterministic targets without sample noise and does not test label noise, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether this makes the curve an ordinary U-shape.
